newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD says globalisation still boiling.
newsitem.headline: OECD says globalisation still boiling.

text.p: Globalisation -- the buzzword for ripping down barriers to international trade and investment -- shows little sign of slowing down and this year could be the biggest yet for cross-border takeovers, says the OECD.

The Paris-based thinktank says direct investment to and from its 29 industrialised countries slipped last year from a 1995 record. But when figures are compiled for the rest of the world's economy they could show that total flows actually rose.

"The continued high level of flows suggests that the process of globalisation brought about in part through international direct investment shows little sign of relenting," the Organisation for Economic Co-operartion and Development said in a report on Financial Market Trends first issued on Sunday.

"The trend towards globalisation is even more pronounced if one looks at cross-border mergers and acquisitions which have grown steadily throughout the 1990s, and look set to continue at historic levels in 1997," it said.
OECD countries invested a total of $259 billion outside their own borders in 1996, down from $289 billion in 1995 but well above the $202 billion seen in 1994.
Money pouring into OECD countries fell to a cumulative total of $198 billion in 1996 from $215 billion the year before, but above the $153 billion in the year before that.
Investment has been chasing after profits seemingly offered by rapid deregulation, privatisation and the removal of monopolies across much of the world throughout the decade.
Privatisations alone hit a record $88 billion last year, of which $68 billion was raiised by OECD countries themselves, the international free-market organisation said.
Other forces include deregulation in telecommunications and airlines and a shift by the world's largest firms towards aggressive expansion in markets which seem to offer quicker prospects for growth.
The OECD said that by far the bulk of investment -- 85 percent in 1995 -- was connected to cross-border mergers and takeovers and the impact of these was likely to continue.
"By all accounts, mergers and acquisitions reached record levels in 1996," it said, adding these could have been worth approximately $263 billion.
British firms invested a record $44 billion abroad in 1996, ranking second as foreign investors behind the United States.

U.S. firms invested $88 billion, down slightly from 1995, while in yen terms Japanese investments grew 20 percent, although remaining at only a third of their peak level of 1990. Outflows from Germany fell.

After a dramatic rise in the late 1980s and an equally fast tumble in the early 1990s, Japanese manufacturing investment has been rising for four years, mainly to Asia and the United States. It has been helped by the appreciation of the yen.
Besides investing abroad, the United States and Britain also remaining the biggest hosts to OECD inward investment, with $84 billion and $33 billion, reaching their shores respectively.
Their combined share of inflows climbed $34 billion in 1996 but this was overshadowed by a $43 billion drop in collective investment to Australia, Germany, Canada and the Netherlands.
Combined net OECD investment to the rest of the world has averaged $60 billion in the 1990s and was $61 billion last year.
